options: water rises upto the top of capillary tube and stays there without overflowing.
water rises upto a point a little below the top and stays there.
water does not rise at all.
water rises upto the tip of capillary tube and then starts overflowing like a fountain.
questions.solution: It won't overflow. That should be obvious since doing so would create a constant flow, constantly using energy, but without any energy input. The same force that pulls the water along the inside of the capillary tube also holds it there when it reaches the end. This force doesn't just pull upward, it pulls the water along the glass. questions.q: The $U$ - tube shown has a uniform cross-section. A liquid is filled in the two arms up to heights ${h}_{1}$ and ${h}_{2}$, and then the liquid is allowed to move. Neglect viscosity and surface tension. When the levels equalize in the two arms, the liquid will
options: Be moving with an acceleration of $\text{g} \left(\dfrac{{h}_{1} - {h}_{2}}{{h}_{1} + {h}_{2} + $$\text{h}$$}\right)$
Exert a net force to the right on the tube.
questions.solution:
When the levels equalize, the height of the liquid in each arm $= \dfrac{{h}_{1} + {h}_{2}}{2}$

We may then visualize that a length ${h}_{1} - \dfrac{{h}_{1} + {h}_{2}}{2} = \dfrac{{h}_{1} - {h}_{2}}{2}$ of the liquid has been transferred from the left arm to the right arm.

Then, the mass of this liquid $= \left(\dfrac{{h}_{1} - {h}_{2}}{2}\right) \text{A} ρ$

where, $A$ = area of tube, $ρ$ = density of the liquid

Distance through which it moves down $= \dfrac{{h}_{1} - {h}_{2}}{2}$

$∴$ Loss in the gravitational potential energy $= {\left(\dfrac{{h}_{1} - {h}_{2}}{2}\right)}^{2} \text{A} ρg$

The mass of the entire liquid $= \left({h}_{1} + {h}_{2} + \text{h}\right) \text{A} ρ$

If this moves with a velocity v, its kinetic energy $= \dfrac{1}{2} \left({h}_{1} + {h}_{2} + \text{h}\right) \text{A} ρ v^{2}$

Equating energies, we get $v = \left({h}_{1} - {h}_{2}\right)\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2\left({h}_{1} + {h}_{2} + \text{h}\right)}}$
